When you launch an open source project in today's world, the biggest dilemma is to decide what software license to use. I'm facing such a dilemma of course, for the side-projects I am maintaining already, and those that I'm yet to launch.

I'm a big supporter of RMS and I ideally want everything to be either GPL or LGPL (though he may not agree with me if I end up choosing MIT/Apache license, lol!).

If I launch it under GPL, the free software community will be most benefited, of course. But at the same time, my software will not be used by a lot of people. For example, people who are already using Apache/MIT/BSD licensed software cannot do a static binding or link it with my GPL code. This is especially true about Android components, since nothing in the Android stack is remotely GPL, and some of my projects are Android apps and libraries. Android uses Bionic instead of glib, Apache Harmony instead of Open JDK, Dalvik instead of JVM, etc.

On the other hand, If I make it as MIT/Apache, first of all, RMS and the FSF will not like it, and people with that ideology may not want to use my software. Secondly, there is also the risk of Appleization of my code happening by the proprietary forces. I'm talking about people who like to modify my work and release as their own closed-source (Apple mindset).

All in all, I'm totally confused as to what license I should release my code under.

I just stumbled across this video that suggests that national debt is good for the citizens.

I suggest chapter 6, entitled, "Credit Diverts Production".

The idea that national debt is good for citizens is a fundamental misunderstanding of what debt is. Debt is the act of pulling future demand forward to the present. In the case of the government creating debt, this is good for the current citizens at the expense of future citizens, maybe even citizens not yet born. The government creating debt and running deficits is effectively the current citizens pulling the demand and consumption of future citizens forward to the present.

The rational case for national debt is creating debt that would lead to an increase in growth large enough to pay for the debt that was created. This concept is susceptible to abuse because government officials can take out debt to provide unsustainable surpluses in the present knowing they will be out of office before the consequences arrive in the future.

There are several reasons economics is misunderstood the largest of which is policymakers and the public seeing success or failure in short term results instead of long term results. Deficit spending will allow society to continue at an unsustainable level of consumption (through corruption or otherwise) by pulling future demand forward until the government becomes insolvent. Society will perceive success in the short term, while deficit spending is ongoing, from artificially elevated benchmarks like equity market indexes or unemployment.

Then all this short term thinking including leaving interest rates at zero to satisfy short term benchmarks has the unintended consequence of creating an excess of marginal commodity producers, which improves the unemployment rate for a time, at the long term expense of massive defaults in high-yield bonds, which savers have fled to because their savings accounts were at zero interest.
